title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
The failure here is a model asserting nonexistent legal authority as fact. An AI legal research tool called Irys generated case citations, case titles, and quoted passages that do not exist, and those fabrications were submitted across multiple court filings without being caught before filing. The error surfaced only because opposing counsel identified the discrepancies and raised them at a hearing, not through any internal review by the filing attorneys.

This is a verification failure at the point of use. The attorneys incorporated AI-generated citations without independently confirming that the cited cases existed in legal databases, which is a step that legal practice has always required even for manually researched sources. The failure mode, a generative model producing plausible but false outputs stated with apparent confidence, is well documented, and the check that would have caught it, looking up each citation before filing, was not performed.

What is not established is whether the AI tool itself lacked safeguards, whether the firm's prior policies required human verification, or what consequences if any the court will impose on counsel. The lead attorney accepted responsibility and stated policies have been updated, but the specifics of those changes are not public.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
State Farm's defense lawyers admitted to using artificial intelligence that generated fake legal cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings in court filings related to a Los Angeles homeowner's lawsuit. The homeowner, Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, sued State Farm and others after a 2020 fire made her Carson home uninhabitable, followed by water damage during repairs. She claimed delays in getting State Farm's approval prevented completion of reconstruction work, forcing her family to drain savings, declare bankruptcy, and lose the home to foreclosure. State Farm's attorney Jacquelene Robinson admitted using an AI tool called Irys and confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not exist, along with incorrect case titles and misquoted passages.

Lead counsel Kenneth Katel accepted responsibility for the errors and stated the firm has updated its AI policies, though specifics were not provided. The discovery came after homeowner's attorney Eric Khodadian presented findings at an August 7 court hearing. A database of legal hallucinations worldwide has documented nearly 1,922 cases, predominantly in the United States, as AI use expands across the legal industry with 41 percent of law firms now using generative AI tools. The trial is scheduled for October.
